opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is basically the problem we've been calling mechanistic anomaly detection. The core worry is that activations are changing all the time. Every new input produces a different pattern, so "the activations look different from training" isn't a useful signal on its own. If you flagged every distributional shift, you'd flag everything, and the system would be useless.

What you actually care about is whether the model is producing its behavior *for the same reason* it did during training. Say you have a model that, on the training distribution, outputs "the diamond is still in the vault" because the diamond really is still in the vault, and the camera reflects that. At deployment, maybe the inputs look totally novel: new lighting, new rooms, whatever. That's fine, as long as the explanation for the output is still "the model saw the diamond, and that caused it to say the diamond is there." The anomaly you want to catch is when the output is the same, but the explanation is different. Maybe someone tampered with the camera, and now the model says "diamond's there" because of the tampering rather than because of the diamond.

So the idea is that you'd have some explanation, something like a heuristic argument, for why the model's behavior on the training distribution has the properties it does. Then for a new input you ask: does that same explanation still account for what's happening here? Ordinary variation in activations is covered by the explanation. The explanation is general; it says "these features combine in this way to produce this output," and that holds across lots of different specific activation values. An anomaly is a case where the explanation fails to cover it, where some term you'd assumed was negligible, some interaction or cancellation, suddenly becomes the thing driving the output.

That's also why I think you can't just do this with simple statistics on activations. A covariance-based detector or something like that will catch some stuff, but it's not tracking causal structure. It can't tell the difference between "this is weird but the mechanism is the same" and "this looks normal on most dimensions, but the mechanism is completely different." And the adversarial cases, the ones you most care about, are exactly the ones where things look normal on the surface.

The hard part, and this is where a lot of our research effort goes, is that we don't really know how to produce these explanations for real neural networks, or even what the right formal object is. You want something like a proof, but proofs are way too strict. Neural nets don't do things for provable reasons; they do things for reasons that are true on average, with a lot of noise. So you need a notion of defeasible, probabilistic argument that's still precise enough that you can check whether it applies to a particular input. If you had that, I think anomaly detection kind of falls out. You compare the explanation's account of a specific case with what's actually happening, and you look at whether the case is "explained the normal way." But getting there is a pretty ambitious theory project, and I'd say we're still fairly early on it.

r001.rationale: It identifies an interaction or cancellation that was assumed negligible becoming the driver of the output as a possible anomaly, against the explanation of ordinary training behavior.

r002.rationale: It says an explanation can cover many different activation values, but does not state that compressing many examples predicts generalization to new examples from the same distribution.

r003.rationale: It says flagging every distributional shift would flag everything and make the system useless.

r004.rationale: It says novel inputs, such as new lighting or rooms, are acceptable when the same explanation still accounts for the output, conveying that such changes need not invalidate the explanation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the heart of what we've been calling mechanistic anomaly detection, and I think the right way to see it is that the explanation itself is the thing that defines "ordinary."

So the setup is something like: you have a model, and on your training distribution it does something you care about. Say it predicts that the sensor readings look fine, or it says the diamond is still in the vault, whatever. And what you'd like is an explanation of why the model produces that behavior on the training distribution. Not a story a human would tell, but some formal object that says: here's the structure in the activations, here's the set of features and the way they interact, that accounts for this output on this distribution. The explanation is meant to be a kind of summary of the mechanisms the model actually uses.

Then at deployment, you get a new input, and the question you ask is not "are the activations different from what I saw in training?" Because the answer to that is always yes. Every input is different. Activations move around constantly, and most of that movement is totally benign. The model is just doing its job on a slightly different input. So raw distance in activation space is a terrible criterion. You'd flag everything.

The question you ask instead is: does this explanation still account for the output on this input? That is, can I take the same mechanism I identified on the training distribution and trace through it on this new input and get the same prediction the model made? If the model says "diamond is still there" and the reason, mechanistically, is the same reason it said that during training — it's seeing the same kind of features and combining them in the same way — then that's an ordinary variation. The activations changed but the explanation covers it.

The anomaly case is when the model produces the output, but the explanation doesn't account for it. The mechanism you identified isn't what's driving the behavior. Maybe some other pathway lit up, maybe there's a feature that was always dormant on the training distribution and now it's active and it's what's actually producing the answer. Classic case is something like the sensors have been tampered with, and the model is predicting "looks fine" not because it's tracking the diamond but because it's tracking the tampering. On the training distribution those two things were correlated, so the model never had to separate them, but the explanation you extracted was about the diamond, and now the thing producing the output is something else.

So the distinction is really about whether the output is produced for the reasons it was produced during training, rather than about how much the internal state moved. And that's nice because it means you don't need to know in advance what the anomaly looks like. You're not building a catalog of bad behaviors. You're just checking that the known good mechanism is still the operative one.

Now, the honest caveat is that this depends enormously on what you mean by an explanation and how you formalize "accounts for." If your explanation is too coarse, it'll cover basically everything and you'll never flag anomalies. If it's too fine, it'll be brittle and flag ordinary inputs. So a lot of the actual work is in getting the right notion of explanation, something that's expressive enough to capture what the model's doing but is actually a summary, where there's a meaningful sense in which it can fail to explain a given case. We've been thinking about this in terms of things like heuristic arguments, where the explanation is a kind of defeasible argument for why the model behaves a certain way, and you can ask whether that argument goes through on a new input. But I'd say that's very much a research program rather than something we know how to do.

r001.rationale: The response describes a different pathway or dormant feature causing anomalous behavior, but does not identify unexpected interactions among circuits used on ordinary inputs.

r002.rationale: It calls the explanation a summary of mechanisms and says to check it on a new input, but does not state that compressing many examples predicts generalization to new examples from the same distribution.

r003.rationale: It says raw activation distance would flag every input because activations vary, but does not state that treating any distribution shift as anomalous would produce near-constant flags.

r004.rationale: The response allows ordinary activation changes when the same explanation still accounts for the output, but does not say that shifts in features irrelevant to the explanation need not invalidate it.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is whether your explanation captures why the model is doing something, rather than just whether its activations look unusual. You should expect activations to change at deployment, because the model is seeing different inputs. And some of those changes will be perfectly benign.

What you’d like is an explanation that says, “This feature of the input caused the model to form this belief, which caused it to take this action.” Then you can ask whether that account still holds at deployment. Is the model responding to new information through mechanisms you understand, or is there some additional consideration driving its behavior?

For example, suppose a model behaves differently because it recognizes that it’s being evaluated. Recognizing an evaluation isn’t itself necessarily concerning. It might need that information to perform the task. The concerning thing would be if that recognition caused it to conceal behavior that it would otherwise exhibit. So it’s the causal role of the information that matters, not merely whether you can find it represented somewhere.

The hard part is establishing that your explanation is faithful and sufficiently complete. You can test it by intervening on the input or on the model and checking whether behavior changes as predicted. But if your explanation leaves out the mechanism responsible for the bad behavior, everything you do explain could look normal. So I’d regard explanations as a way to make a more targeted anomaly detector, rather than something that automatically solves the problem.

r001.rationale: It discusses benign activation changes and causal explanations, but does not identify unexpected interactions among circuits used on ordinary inputs as a possible source of anomalous behavior.

r002.rationale: It does not state that an explanation compressing many examples should generalize to new examples from the same distribution.

r003.rationale: It says some deployment activation changes are benign, but does not explain that flagging every distribution shift would produce near-constant anomaly flags.

r004.rationale: It does not state that shifts in features irrelevant to an explanation need not invalidate it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: a change relative to what? You shouldn’t expect the activations at deployment to look just like the activations in training. The model is seeing new things, and some of those differences are precisely what you want it to respond to.

What you’d like is an explanation of why the model took an action that continues to work across those changes. Suppose your explanation is that the model answers a question by finding relevant information and using it to infer the answer. Then encountering a new fact will change its activations, but that’s compatible with your explanation. If instead it starts answering differently because it believes it’s no longer being evaluated, that could be a failure of the explanation, even if the change in activations is quite small.

So I’d want to turn the explanation into predictions you can test, including by intervening on the model or changing the situation. Does changing the evidence change the answer in the way you expect? Does changing whether the model thinks it’s being watched affect its behavior?

The hard part is that an explanation can be good enough to predict all the behavior you’ve observed and still leave out something important. So this isn’t automatically a solution to the deployment problem. You need some reason to believe your tests distinguish the explanation you intended from alternatives that agree during testing and come apart later.

r001.rationale: The response discusses activation changes and possible behavioral failures, but does not identify unexpected interactions among circuits used on ordinary inputs as a source of anomalies.

r002.rationale: It does not say that explanations compress many examples or that this predicts generalization to new examples from the same distribution.

r003.rationale: It does not explain that flagging every distribution shift would make anomaly flags nearly constant.

r004.rationale: It says a new fact can change activations while remaining compatible with an explanation, but does not state that shifts in features irrelevant to the explanation need not invalidate it.
